articles.title: Fed hikes ahead, but not just yet
articles.summary: San Francisco: The Federal Reserve will probably need to increase short-term interest rates further to rein in too-high inflation, San Francisco Federal Reserve President Mary Daly said on Wednesday, but she also signaled there's no need to do so at the US central bank's October 27-28 meeting."We are more likely than not to need additional adjustments, but the timing of those adjustments to me is something we're still deliberating," Daly told Reuters in an interview. "I don't feel urgent that we have to decide with a limited set of information. I think we have the time that we need."Also Read: US inflation worsened last month to 3.7% in sign that prices remain elevated as midterm elections nearSeveral of Daly's colleagues have also signaled in recent weeks that the Fed is unlikely to raise rates this month. The Fed's policy rate is in the 3.75%-4.00% range, and longer-term borrowing costs are even higher, with some -- like 7.5% mortgage rates -- putting an increasingly obvious damper on demand in some parts of the economy.Daly said she feels financial markets understand the Fed's "reaction function," pointing to how traders responded to data earlier on Wednesday that showed consumer price inflation accelerated to 3.7% in the 12 months through September, a bit faster than economists had anticipated. The Fed targets 2% inflation by a different, but related, measure.Though the initial reaction was "robust," she said -- rate futures traders quickly piled into bets on an October Fed rate hike -- investors "calmed" after parsing through the data. Higher gasoline prices drove the overall increase, and underlying inflation, while still sticky, did not take a sharp turn upward."Definitely this data point suggests that the risk to inflation remains elevated," Daly said. "The risk to inflation has gone up more, but risks are not realities, and reacting on risk when you have time to make a good decision, to me, feels imprudent."Also Read: More expensive gas, semiconductors likely pushed up inflation in US last monthDaly said that the labor market's continued stability gives the Fed room to focus on price stability.But, she said, "why force urgency when you don't need to have urgency? Why not take the time to be thoughtful and deliberate? And we have more meetings ahead of us."Financial market pricing now puts about a 40% chance of a second straight Fed rate hike at the central bank's next meeting, up from before the data but no longer seeing an increase as the most likely outcome.

articles.summary: India’s IT-BPM sector is set to revive fresher hiring after a sharp contraction, but the recovery is rewiring the skills companies seek in graduates.Fresher hiring in the sector is projected to rise to up to 2.1 lakh in FY27, after falling to an estimated 1.75 lakh in FY26 from 4 lakh in FY22, according to technology consulting and talent advisory firm HAN Digital’s IT-BPM Graduate Hiring Outlook 2027.However, demand is increasingly shifting towards artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), data engineering, cybersecurity and other specialised technology roles, away from conventional entry-level coding and business process outsourcing jobs.IT Services players will remain the largest employers of the sector’s freshers, accounting for about 60% of hires, though growth now will be concentrated in AI-adjacent and specialised roles.GCCs are the fastest-growing channel, expected to recruit 28% of talent as they expand intake into Tier II/III cities. Pure-play BPOs’ share keeps shrinking, mirroring the shift from routine execution to specialised, AI-adjacent work.“The rise in fresher hiring reflects a structural reset in how IT services firms are building their talent pyramid,” said Saravanan Balasundaram, CEO, HAN Digital Solution.As system integrators and IT Service providers sign more AI, data engineering and AI-enabled deals with existing and new clients, the bench capacity reduced by layoffs over the last few years can no longer absorb the demand, he said. “At the same time, new AI roles in data engineering, AI testing, annotation and model operations are opening up at the base of the pyramid, where AI-ready graduates can be skilled and deployed at scale, while mid-level hiring in the four+ years band remains under cost and productivity pressure.”The shift is changing expectations from new recruits. As AI tools take over parts of routine coding, testing and repetitive tasks, employers increasingly want graduates who can work with AI systems, validate their outputs and apply technology to business problems.The skillsets that companies are hiring for are definitely changing, said Sangeeta Gupta, senior VP, Nasscom. “It’s much more focused on AI capabilities – there are new jobs that are also opening up with data centres coming up.”The traditional model of bulk hiring, six months of training and deployment is also changing. “The new kind of freshers companies need are AI-native,” she said.This change is also visible in salaries. Freshers with AI-allied skills can command significantly higher pay, indicating that employers are increasingly paying for specialised skills rather than graduate headcount alone.India’s Tier-1 IT Services players’ 2027 fresher model offers Rs 12–22 lakh for select specialised engineers in AI, data engineering, cybersecurity and enterprise tech as the premium shifts toward specialised technology capability, found the report.“This would never happen in the past,” said Gupta, citing Infosys’ plan to offer up to Rs 21 lakh for certain specialised tech roles. Entry-level salaries across ITeS meanwhile have largely stagnated at Rs 3-4 lakh for years.Recruitment geography is widening too. Bengaluru remains the leading fresher destination, accounting for an estimated 25% of onboarding, followed by Delhi-NCR at 17%, Hyderabad at 16%, Chennai at 15% and Mumbai and Pune at 10% each. Yet, Tier 2/3 corridors are outpacing metro growth, albeit on a smaller base, at 35% year-on-year.Coimbatore, Jaipur, Kochi, Indore, Ahmedabad, and Visakhapatnam are attracting freshers via local GCC centres and IT services players seeking lower-cost talent pools beyond major metros.
